decision.question: Should I take medication to lower my blood pressure, or focus on lifestyle changes first?

options.label: Take lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) daily

benefits.outcome: Major cardiovascular event prevented (heart attack, stroke, heart failure, or cardiovascular death)

evidence.source: Ettehad D et al. Lancet 2016 (meta-analysis, n=413,000); Blood Pressure Lowering Treatment Trialists Collaboration, Lancet 2021. A 10 mmHg SBP reduction yields approximately 27% relative risk reduction in major CV events. A typical ACE inhibitor achieves 8–10 mmHg average reduction.
evidence.population_caveat: NNT varies substantially by baseline risk. At SBP 130–139 mmHg (lower stage 1), the absolute benefit is roughly half — NNT ~130. At SBP 150–159 mmHg or with additional risk factors (diabetes, CKD, prior CV disease), NNT approaches 25–40. Your clinician can calculate your 10-year ASCVD risk to sharpen this estimate.

evidence.source: Ettehad D et al. Lancet 2016: RR 0.73 per 10 mmHg SBP reduction (27% relative reduction). Law M et al. BMJ 2009 (147 trials, n=464,000) confirm similar stroke reduction.
evidence.population_caveat: Stroke reduction is one of the most consistent benefits across all antihypertensive classes. Benefit is proportional to the achieved blood pressure reduction.

evidence.source: Ettehad D et al. Lancet 2016: RR 0.72 per 10 mmHg SBP reduction (28% relative reduction in heart failure).
evidence.population_caveat: Heart failure benefit is particularly strong with ACE inhibitors and ARBs compared to other drug classes, likely due to effects beyond blood pressure lowering alone.

harms.outcome: Dry cough requiring stopping the medication (ACE inhibitor class effect)

evidence.source: Dicpinigaitis PV. Chest 2006 (review); Singapore primary care cohort (PMC4293986). Cough occurs in ~10% of patients; approximately 5% stop the drug because of it. Switching to an ARB (e.g. losartan) eliminates cough entirely — it is a class effect of ACE inhibitors, not a sign of an allergic reaction.
evidence.population_caveat: Cough is more common in women and in people of East Asian ancestry (up to 30–40% incidence). It resolves completely within days of stopping the drug.

harms.outcome: Acute kidney injury or significant creatinine rise

evidence.source: SPRINT trial, NEJM 2015 (n=9,361): AKI or creatinine doubling 4.1% vs 2.5% over 3.2 years. Most episodes are mild and reversible on dose reduction or stopping the drug.
evidence.population_caveat: Risk is substantially higher in people with pre-existing chronic kidney disease or who are taking NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) regularly. Routine creatinine monitoring at 1–4 weeks after starting is standard practice.

harms.outcome: Symptomatic low blood pressure — dizziness or lightheadedness

evidence.source: SPRINT trial, NEJM 2015: symptomatic hypotension 2.4% vs 1.4% intensive vs standard (extrapolated to medication vs lifestyle). ALLHAT trial (n=33,357) provides broader context.
evidence.population_caveat: Dizziness is most common when first starting the medication or after dose increases. Usually manageable with timing (take at night) or dose adjustment. Falls risk is a concern in adults over 75 — discuss this explicitly with your clinician.

harms.outcome: Angioedema (sudden swelling of the face, lips, or throat — rare but serious)
harms.cascade: Angioedema can obstruct the airway and is a medical emergency. It typically occurs within the first weeks of starting the drug. If swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat occurs, stop the drug immediately and call 911. Switching to an ARB (e.g. losartan) largely eliminates this risk.

evidence.source: Brown NJ, Vaughan DE. Circulation 1998; ACE inhibitor vs ARB comparative data from ONTARGET (NEJM 2008). Incidence ~0.1–0.7% over 5 years; higher in Black patients (~3×) and in those with prior angioedema.
evidence.population_caveat: Risk is substantially higher in Black patients. If you have a history of angioedema from any cause, ACE inhibitors should generally be avoided — an ARB is the preferred alternative.

options.burden: One tablet taken daily, typically in the morning or evening. Standard monitoring: renal function and potassium at 1–4 weeks after starting, then annually. Blood pressure check at 4–8 weeks to confirm response. Cost: ~$4–10/month for generic lisinopril. If cough develops, your clinician will typically switch you to losartan (an ARB), which works similarly without the cough.
unknowns: Whether people with SBP 130–139 mmHg (the lower end of stage 1 by 2017 ACC/AHA guidelines) benefit meaningfully from medication — most major trials enrolled patients with SBP ≥140 mmHg, and the absolute benefit at 130–139 is uncertain.

How much of the long-term cardiovascular risk reduction comes from blood pressure lowering itself versus other effects of ACE inhibitors (anti-inflammatory, kidney-protective properties) — this affects whether switching drug classes changes the benefit.

Whether the SPRINT findings (showing benefit of very intensive BP control to <120 mmHg) apply broadly — SPRINT used automated office BP measurement, which typically reads 5–10 mmHg lower than conventional measurement, making direct comparison to standard practice complex.

How fall risk in older adults (especially over 75) should factor into the medication decision — the evidence on falls from antihypertensives is mixed, but conservative dosing and nighttime administration may reduce this risk.

options.label: Lifestyle changes — no medication

evidence.source: Dicpinigaitis PV. Chest 2006; Singapore cohort PMC4293986. Avoiding the drug avoids the cough entirely.
evidence.population_caveat: This benefit is specific to ACE inhibitors. If medication is ultimately needed, choosing an ARB (losartan) instead eliminates this side effect.

benefits.outcome: Avoid acute kidney stress from medication

evidence.source: SPRINT trial, NEJM 2015. Avoiding antihypertensives avoids the small excess risk of medication-related creatinine rise.
evidence.population_caveat: Uncontrolled hypertension itself is a major cause of kidney disease over the long term — the kidney benefit of avoiding medication is short-term, while the harm of untreated hypertension to the kidneys accumulates over years.

harms.outcome: Major cardiovascular event — higher rate without medication (heart attack, stroke, heart failure, or cardiovascular death)
harms.cascade: Heart attack and stroke can cause permanent disability or death. Heart failure significantly limits activity and quality of life and requires ongoing treatment. Untreated high blood pressure is the leading modifiable risk factor for stroke worldwide.

evidence.source: Ettehad D et al. Lancet 2016; BPLTTC Lancet 2021. Mirror of the medication benefit — same data, opposite framing.
evidence.population_caveat: Risk varies greatly by baseline SBP and individual cardiovascular risk. At SBP 130–139 mmHg and low overall ASCVD risk, the 5-year absolute risk difference is smaller. The harm of untreated hypertension compounds over decades.

options.burden: DASH diet (high fruits, vegetables, low sodium — targets <1,500 mg sodium/day), regular aerobic exercise (150 min/week moderate intensity), weight loss if overweight (each 1 kg lost reduces SBP ~1 mmHg), limiting alcohol. Together these changes can reduce SBP by 10–15 mmHg in motivated patients — comparable to a single medication — but sustained adherence is challenging. Blood pressure monitoring every 3–6 months to track response. If BP remains elevated after 3–6 months of lifestyle change, most guidelines recommend adding medication.
unknowns: Whether lifestyle modification alone can sustain adequate BP control over 5+ years without medication — adherence typically declines over time, and BP often rises gradually even with initial success.

How much of the long-term cardiovascular risk reduction from blood pressure control requires sustained treatment vs. periodic control — there is little data on 'lifestyle then medication if needed' as a structured strategy.
Whether specific dietary patterns (Mediterranean vs. DASH vs. low-carbohydrate) differ meaningfully in their sustained blood pressure effects beyond 1–2 years.
